title: Florida Store Owner Charged With Murder After Teen E-Bike Rider Dies
excerpt: West Melbourne police say Kavan Patel, 32, intentionally struck 14-year-old Hunter Russey after a store burglary alarm and left him in a ditch; the boy died days later.
body:
• Kavan Vishnubhai Patel, 32, a West Melbourne convenience store owner, faces a second-degree murder charge in the death of 14-year-old Hunter Russey, police said.
  • Police say Patel followed the teenager on an e-bike after a burglary alarm at his store on October 13, intentionally struck him with his vehicle and left the scene.
  • Russey was found hours later in a roadside ditch with multiple skull fractures and died after his family removed life support; his organs were donated.
  • Patel is held at Brevard County jail without bond after re-arrest on October 18; he was first charged with aggravated battery and leaving the scene.

A Florida convenience store owner has been charged with second-degree murder after police say he intentionally struck a 14-year-old boy riding an e-bike whom he believed had tried to break into his shop, and left him in a roadside ditch. Kavan Vishnubhai Patel, 32, was re-arrested on October 18 after Hunter Russey died, according to the West Melbourne Police Department reporting cited by the New York Post.

What police say happened

Officers were called to the Corner Store on Wickham Road in West Melbourne at about 4:30 a.m. on October 13 after an alarm indicated a possible burglary, police said in a press release reported by Internewscast. Patel told police his security company had notified him of a break-in, that surveillance showed the store's front glass door shattered, and that he drove to the store and followed a person fleeing on an e-bike before losing sight of him.

Investigators said that account was not accurate. Not far from the store, officers found Russey lying in the roadway, matching the description Patel had given. Nearby video recorded the sound of a vehicle hitting the boy, followed by impacts with a mailbox and trash cans, and police observed damage to the front of Patel's vehicle. When confronted, Patel allegedly admitted following Russey and hitting him, telling officers he knew he should have called police but was "angry," investigators wrote.

"He continues to follow him, doesn't call law enforcement, doesn't notify law enforcement that this is going on, and at some point runs into the bicyclist trying to stop him."

— Lt. Graig Erenstoft, West Melbourne Police Department, to WESH

From battery charge to murder charge

Russey was found unresponsive with multiple skull fractures and taken to Orlando Health's Arnold Palmer Hospital, where he was placed on life support. His family removed life support on Saturday and he died; the family chose to donate his organs. Patel was initially charged with aggravated battery and leaving the scene of a crash involving great bodily injury. After Russey's death, he was arrested again on October 18 and charged with second-degree murder, and is being held at Brevard County jail without bond.

The charges are allegations; Patel has not been convicted. For Indian-origin store owners across Florida and the wider diaspora — a community heavily represented in US convenience retail — the case is a stark reminder of the line the law draws: police say a suspected burglary is a call to law enforcement, and taking pursuit into your own hands can convert a property crime report into a homicide prosecution. The case will proceed through Brevard County court, where the arrest affidavit's account will be tested against the surveillance and vehicle evidence investigators say they hold.
